questions.question: What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it in Ruby/Rails?
questions.title: SQL Injection Basics
questions.direct_answer: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string: `User.where("name = '#{params[:name]}'")` lets an attacker pass `'; DROP TABLE users; --` and run arbitrary SQL. Prevent it with PARAMETERIZED queries / placeholders — never interpolate user input. In Rails, `User.where(name: params[:name])` is safe (Active Record binds the value); `User.where("name = ?", params[:name])` is safe too (? is a placeholder). Never use string interpolation (`"...#{params[:x]}"`) or `.to_sql` with user input. The danger: an attacker can read all data, change it, or drop tables. The fix is always the same: keep data separate from code — use bound parameters so the DB treats input as a value, not SQL. Validate input too, but parameterization is the real defense.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know SQL injection is string-concatenated input and that parameterized queries / placeholders prevent it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Interpolating user input into a SQL string (use placeholders/binders instead).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: SQL injection = concatenating input into SQL. Prevent with parameterized queries (where(name: x) or where("...?", x)). Never interpolate into a SQL string.

sections.title: Separate Data from Code
sections.content: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string: User where name equals params name lets an attacker pass quote semicolon DROP TABLE users semicolon dash dash and run arbitrary SQL. Prevent it with PARAMETERIZED queries or placeholders — never interpolate user input. In Rails, User where name params name is safe (Active Record binds the value); User where name question mark params name is safe too (question mark is a placeholder). Never use string interpolation (dot dot dot params x) or to_sql with user input. The danger: an attacker can read all data, change it, or drop tables. The fix is always the same: keep data separate from code — use bound parameters so the DB treats input as a value, not SQL. Validate input too, but parameterization is the real defense.

sections.title: SQL Injection
sections.content:
input concatenated into SQL. Prevent with placeholders/binders. Never interpolate.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[bad: "...#{params[:name]}"] --> I[inject: '; DROP TABLE]
  G[good: where(name: x) or where("=?", x)] --> P[bound parameter]
  P --> S[DB treats as VALUE, not SQL]
```

sections.title: SQL injection
sections.content:
```ruby
# BAD: string interpolation -> SQL injection
# User.where("name = '#{params[:name]}'")
#   attacker sends:  name = '; DROP TABLE users; --
#   SQL becomes:     name = ''; DROP TABLE users; --'
# User.where("age > #{params[:age]}")              # also bad
# User.find_by_sql("SELECT * WHERE name='#{x}'")   # also bad

# GOOD: parameterized / placeholders (Active Record binds the value)
User.where(name: params[:name])                # hash form (safe)
User.where('name = ?', params[:name])           # ? placeholder (safe)
User.where('name = :n', n: params[:name])       # named placeholder (safe)
User.where('age > ?', params[:age])             # safe

# Why it works: the DB treats the bound value as DATA, not SQL.
# An attacker's  '; DROP TABLE users; --  is just a weird NAME string.

# Raw SQL with user input -> still avoid; if you must, bind:
User.find_by_sql(['SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?', params[:name]])

# Rule: NEVER interpolate/concatenate user input into a SQL string.
# Validate input too, but PARAMETERIZATION is the real defense.
# Keep data separate from code.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Interpolating user input into a SQL string (use placeholders/binders).
Assuming validation alone prevents injection (parameterization is the real defense).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: SQL injection: concatenating untrusted input into a SQL string lets an attacker run arbitrary SQL.
Prevent with parameterized queries: where(name: x) or where('name = ?', x) (Active Record binds).
Never interpolate user input into a SQL string ("...#{params[:x]}").
The DB treats a bound value as data, not SQL — an attacker's payload becomes a weird string.
Validate input too, but parameterization is the real defense (keep data separate from code).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string: User where name equals params name lets an attacker pass quote semicolon DROP TABLE users semicolon dash dash and run arbitrary SQL. Prevent it with PARAMETERIZED queries or placeholders — never interpolate user input. In Rails, User where name params name is safe (Active Record binds the value); user where name question mark params name is safe too (question mark is a placeholder). Never use string interpolation (dot dot dot params x) or to_sql with user input. The danger: an attacker can read all data, change it, or drop tables. The fix is always the same: keep data separate from code — use bound parameters so the DB treats input as a value, not SQL. Validate input too, but parameterization is the real defense. A common mistake is interpolating user input into a SQL string, when you should use placeholders or binders.
